In the nearshore rocky habitats of the North Pacific, the masked greenling (Hexagrammos octogrammus) exhibits life-history traits characteristic of a territorial, nest-guarding cottid relative. Field surveys indicate that neonates emerge from demersal eggs at a very small size, with a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams]. This minute mass reflects the modest egg diameter of roughly 1.75 millimeters, which provides a limited yolk reserve that sustains the lecithotrophic larva only until the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-dependent prolarva undergoes rapid initial growth within the first few days following eclosion, relying entirely on endogenous nutrients absorbed from the yolk sac. Once the exotrophic transition is complete, the free-swimming larva begins actively foraging on small zooplankton, marking a critical shift toward somatic development that will eventually lead to the attainment of a much larger adult body size. Comparative data from related hexagrammids suggest that this early life stage is particularly vulnerable to starvation, as the point of no return is reached quickly if prey is unavailable.

At approximately 15.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15.5 centimeters] in total length, individuals attain puberty, with a corresponding body mass of 52.5 grams [Wwp = 52.5 grams] marking the pubertal transition. This length threshold is typically reached within the first two to three years of life, after which post-pubertal adults may continue to grow, albeit at a slower rate. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is marked by the initiation of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, which prepares the spawning adult for the reproductive season. Field observations indicate that nest-guarding males establish territories among boulder and cobble substrates, where they attract gravid females for broadcast spawning events. The timing of this first spawning is closely tied to seasonal temperature regimes, which modulate the rate of gonad maturation.

The maximum recorded longevity for this species under natural conditions has been documented at twelve years [am = twelve years], a lifespan that places it among the longer-lived members of the Hexagrammidae when maintained at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable for a fish of its size and reflects the relatively slow pace of life history typical of high-latitude marine teleosts. Senescent adults in the oldest age classes show signs of reduced fecundity and diminished nest-guarding success, suggesting that reproductive senescence may set in during the final years of life. Growth asymptotes gradually, with the largest adults attaining an ultimate total length of up to 42 centimeters [Li = up to 42 centimeters] under favorable foraging conditions, a size that is among the largest recorded for the genus Hexagrammos and reflects the extended growth period afforded by the species' relatively long lifespan.

Reproductive output in the masked greenling has been examined through field-based fecundity estimates and laboratory observations of spawning frequency. Drawing on data from the closely related species Hexagrammos stelleri, which occupies a similar thermal niche, the fecundity per spawning event is estimated at approximately 38,400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 38,400 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring once per year [F_R_i = spawning occurring once per year] when maintained at a temperature of 9.39 °C [T = 9.39 °C]. The chorionate embryos develop within the nest for several weeks, during which time the attending male fans the egg mass to maintain oxygen flow and prevent fungal infection. Such paternal care is energetically costly and may limit the number of successful spawning events a male can manage within a single breeding season. Post-hatch, the yolk-sac larva emerges synchronously, initiating the planktonic phase of the life cycle.

Habitat selection by the benthic juvenile following larval metamorphosis is a critical determinant of recruitment success. Recently metamorphosed juveniles settle preferentially in shallow, structurally complex habitats dominated by macroalgae and cobble, which provide refuge from piscivorous predators. The post-settlement juvenile then enters a period of rapid somatic growth, during which the body plan is reorganized from the compressed larval form to the more robust, elongated adult morphology characteristic of the genus. This allometric shift is accompanied by the development of the distinctive cirri above the eyes that give the masked greenling its common name. Growth rates during the juvenile stage are strongly influenced by local prey abundance and water temperature, with slower growth observed at the cooler end of the species thermal range. The fingerling stage persists until the onset of sexual maturation, at which point the fish transitions morphologically and behaviorally toward the territorial, spawning adult stage, completing the life cycle.
